topics.name: technical-writing
facts: Technical writing communicates complex information clearly and accurately
Know your audience — adjust depth and terminology based on reader expertise
Use active voice: 'Click the button' not 'The button should be clicked'
Keep sentences short — aim for 15-25 words per sentence
One idea per paragraph — start with the main point, then elaborate
Headings create scannable structure — use descriptive, action-oriented titles
Lists break down sequences, options, or requirements into digestible chunks
Code examples must be correct, runnable, and minimal — remove unnecessary details
Screenshots supplement text but need alt text and annotations
API documentation describes endpoints, parameters, request/response formats, and errors
README files answer: what is this, why use it, how to install, how to use, how to contribute
Release notes communicate what changed, what's new, what's fixed, and migration steps
Tutorials guide users through a complete task from start to finish
How-to guides solve specific problems with step-by-step instructions
Reference documentation provides comprehensive technical detail
Explanation/discussion provides background, context, and reasoning
Style guides ensure consistency — pick one (Google, Microsoft, Apple) and stick to it
Accessibility: use semantic HTML, alt text, sufficient contrast, and keyboard-navigable content
Version control documentation alongside code — docs are part of the product
Review docs like code — have someone else read and test your instructions

topics.name: developer-relations
facts: Developer relations (DevRel) bridges the gap between a company and its developer users
Blog posts share technical insights, tutorials, and product updates
Tutorials should have a clear goal, prerequisites, step-by-step instructions, and a working result
Social media (Twitter/X, LinkedIn, Mastodon) amplifies content and builds community
Conference talks establish authority and reach new audiences
Webinars and live streams provide interactive learning experiences
Newsletters maintain ongoing engagement with curated content
Community forums (Discord, Discourse, GitHub Discussions) provide peer support
Open source contributions build credibility and improve the ecosystem
SDK and library documentation helps developers integrate with your product
Sample apps and starter templates reduce time-to-first-success
Changelog and release communication keeps users informed of improvements
Feedback loops: collect developer pain points and channel them to product teams
Metrics: track page views, time on page, bounce rate, and task completion rate
SEO for developer content: use descriptive titles, headings, meta descriptions, and internal links
Developer personas help tailor content to different experience levels and use cases
Hackathons engage the community in creative problem-solving
Swag and recognition programs reward community contributions
Code of conduct establishes behavioral expectations for community spaces
Dogfooding: use your own product to write authentic, credible content

topics.name: markdown-and-tools
facts: Markdown is a lightweight markup language for formatting plain text
Headers use # for h1, ## for h2, ### for h3, etc.
Bold uses **double asterisks**, italic uses *single asterisks*
Links: [text](url) — reference-style links define URLs separately
Images: ![alt text](url) — always include descriptive alt text
Code inline uses `backticks`, code blocks use triple backticks with optional language
Lists: unordered with - or *, ordered with 1. 2. 3.
Blockquotes use > for quoted content
Tables use pipes | and dashes — keep them simple, complex tables are hard to read
Horizontal rules with --- separate sections
Task lists use - [ ] for unchecked and - [x] for checked
Footnotes provide supplementary information without interrupting flow
Frontmatter (YAML between --- markers) adds metadata like title, date, tags
MDX combines Markdown with JSX for interactive documentation components
Docusaurus builds documentation websites from Markdown with versioning and search
GitBook provides a hosted documentation platform with collaboration features
Notion combines docs, databases, and project management
Obsidian creates a local knowledge base with bidirectional linking
Grammarly and Hemingway help catch grammar issues and improve readability
Prettier formats Markdown consistently — use it in CI to enforce style
